docs.title: Pyntegrate
docs.text:
Integrative analysis of high-throughput sequencing data.

Pyntegrate is a Python library for genomic data analysis, built on the foundation of metaseq, created by Ryan Dale. It extends that foundation to analyze and cross-compare a wider variety of data types (ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and DNase-seq/ATAC-seq) through a single, consistent API, and turns each common analysis into a one-call pipeline that returns publication-ready matplotlib figures.

Install Pyntegrate Getting Started Examples

docs.title: Why Pyntegrate?
docs.text:
Integrating several sequencing assays usually means juggling a different tool, file format, and plotting script for each one. Pyntegrate brings them under one roof:

  • Multi-omics integration

    Combine ChIP-seq signal, ATAC-seq accessibility, and RNA-seq differential expression in the same analysis: split heatmaps by expression status, correlate log2 fold changes across assays, or group genes into ATAC/RNA quadrants.

  • One-call pipelines

    Each analysis is a pipeline class: pass file paths and parameters, call .run(), and get back ready-to-save figures. No separate loading, binning, or plotting step.

  • Rich visualization

    Heatmaps, meta-gene profiles, dual-axis overlays, volcano plots, decile boxplots, violin plots, hexbin correlations, and circos plots out of the box.

  • Format-agnostic signal

    A uniform interface to read BigWig, BAM, BigBed, BED, and NarrowPeak files, plus DESeq2/edgeR-style result tables, with CPM normalization handled for you.

  • Gene and peak annotation

    Classify genomic regions (promoter, intergenic, ...) from interval data and, optionally, call and annotate peaks through HOMER.

  • Low-level access when you need it

    Every pipeline is built from public building blocks (SignalArrayGenerator, Plotting, Filtering, ...) that you can call directly for custom workflows.

docs.title: Supported Data Types
docs.text: Data type Typical input What Pyntegrate does with it ChIP-seq BigWig / BAM Signal extraction around TSS, IP − INPUT subtraction, heatmaps, profiles, log2FC correlations RNA-seq CSV/TSV (DESeq2-style) Differential-expression parsing, volcano plots, decile and violin analysis, up/down gene splits DNase-seq / ATAC-seq BigWig / BAM / CSV Accessibility signal extraction, category heatmaps, overlay profiles, knockdown correlations

docs.title: Supported file formats
docs.text: Format Support level bigwig, bam Full functionality, including read counting and signal extraction bed, bigbed, narrowPeak, gff, gtf, vcf Most functionality, but no read counting csv / tsv Full functionality for differential-expression tables (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq log2FC) gffutils .db Gene annotation database used to locate TSSs and gene bodies

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Signal files<br/>BigWig / BAM / BED] --> P
    B[Annotations<br/>gffutils .db] --> P
    C[DE tables<br/>CSV / TSV] --> P
    P["Pipeline<br/>(e.g. IntegratedHeatmapPipeline)"] -->|".run()"| F[matplotlib Figures]
    F --> S[".savefig()<br/>PNG / SVG / PDF"]
  1. Point a pipeline at your files. Signal tracks, a gene annotation database, and (where relevant) differential-expression tables.
  2. Call .run(). The pipeline reads the files, normalizes signal, builds binned arrays around TSSs or gene bodies, merges in expression or accessibility status, and draws the plots.
  3. Save or tweak the figures. You get standard matplotlib.figure.Figure objects, so anything matplotlib can do still applies.

docs.title: A 30-second Example
docs.text:
Compare ChIP-seq IP vs. INPUT signal around every annotated TSS:

from Pyntegrate.pipelines import PeakHeatmapPipeline

pipe = PeakHeatmapPipeline(
    db_path="annotations.gtf.db",   # gffutils FeatureDB
    ip_path="ip_signal.bw",
    input_path="input_signal.bw",
    genome="mm10",
    window=(-1000, 1000),
    bins=100,
)
figs = pipe.run()   # dict of matplotlib Figures

figs["profile"].savefig("profile.png", dpi=300)
figs["heatmap_sorted_mean"].savefig("heatmap.png", dpi=300)

The Getting Started guide walks through this and the RNA-seq / ATAC-seq integration pipelines step by step.

docs.title: Available Pipelines
docs.text:
All pipelines live in Pyntegrate.pipelines and follow the same instantiate → .run() → figures pattern.

Category Pipeline Output Signal around TSS PeakHeatmapPipeline IP − INPUT profile and heatmaps (unsorted, sorted by mean, sorted by max) CategoryHeatmapPipeline Signal heatmaps split by genomic category GeneScaleRegionsProfilePipeline Meta-profile over scaled gene bodies Multi-omics integration IntegratedHeatmapPipeline Signal heatmap and profile split by RNA-seq or ATAC-seq up/down status OverlayProfilePipeline Dual-axis average-profile overlay (e.g. ChIP vs. ATAC) GeneGroupProfilePipeline Average signal profile split by ATAC/RNA log2FC quadrants MultiSignalComparisonPipeline Multi-modal log2FC scatter plots CircPlotPipeline Circos plot comparing changes across several signals Differential analysis VolcanoPipeline Volcano plot from differential-expression results RNAViolinPipeline RNA expression violins with significance overlay DecilePipeline Signal decile boxplot with expression overlay (signal files + gene DB) DecileScatterPipeline CSV-only decile analysis with flexible column selection Correlations ChIPCategoryCorrelationPipeline Hexbin ChIP-seq correlation filtered by category RNAKnockdownCorrelationPipeline Hexbin RNA-seq correlation for significant knockdown genes ATACKnockdownCorrelationPipeline Hexbin ATAC-seq correlation for significant knockdown peaks

docs.title: Case Study: FACT Knockdown
docs.text: The examples/ directory reproduces a complete integrative analysis of a knockdown of the FACT histone chaperone complex (subunits SSRP1 and SUPT16H), combining ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq. There is one self-contained script per figure, each with a configuration block at the top and a docstring describing the workflow. It is the best place to see how the pipelines fit together on real data.

docs.title: Package Overview
docs.text: Module Purpose Reference Pyntegrate.pipelines High-level, one-call analysis pipelines (recommended entry point) Pipelines Pyntegrate.SeqSignalAnalysis Building blocks used by the pipelines: signal arrays, plotting, filtering, HOMER wrappers, annotation helpers SeqSignalAnalysis Pyntegrate._genomic_signal Uniform readers for BigWig, BAM, BigBed, BED, and NarrowPeak signal Genomic Signal Pyntegrate.results_table DESeq2 / edgeR differential-expression result tables Results Table Pyntegrate.helpers, array_helpers, colormap_adjust Utilities for arrays, file handling, and colormaps Helpers

docs.title: Requirements at a Glance
docs.text:
• Python 3.9-3.12 (3.10 recommended). numpy 1.26 and pybedtools 0.9.1 do not build on 3.13+
  • bedtools on your PATH (and samtools for BAM workflows)
  • Optional: HOMER, only for peak calling and peak annotation

All Python dependencies are installed automatically by pip. See Installation for Conda, venv, and one-command setup options.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: This gallery walks through the runnable example scripts in examples/. Each script reproduces one figure (or figure panel) from a FACT (SSRP1/SUPT16H) knockdown ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq/RNA-seq analysis, wrapping one Pyntegrate pipeline end-to-end — from raw signal/expression files to a saved figure. Every script follows the same shape: a Configuration section at the top, a docstring explaining the workflow, one or more pipeline calls, and an OUTPUT_PATH (saved to outputs/figs/ at 300 dpi).

docs.title: Figure 1 — Meta-gene Profile and Cross-modality Correlations
docs.text:
Pipelines: GeneScaleRegionsProfilePipeline, ChIPCategoryCorrelationPipeline, RNAKnockdownCorrelationPipeline, ATACKnockdownCorrelationPipeline, PeakHeatmapPipeline

Five independent panels: a deepTools-style scaled-gene-body meta-profile (1A), two hexbin correlations between the SSRP1 and SUPT16H knockdowns for ChIP, RNA and ATAC log2 fold-changes (1B–1D), and a ChIP-seq IP vs. INPUT profile on a separate dataset (1E).

1A — Meta-gene profile1B — ChIP correlation1C — RNA knockdown correlation1D — ATAC knockdown correlation1E — ChIP IP vs INPUT profile

Scales every annotated gene body to a common length with fixed-length upstream/downstream flanks and averages SSRP1 vs. SUPT16H ChIP-seq signal across all genes.

Script: Fig 1A.py

Hexbin density scatter correlating SSRP1 vs. SUPT16H ChIP log2 fold-change at TSS windows classified as FACT-high in at least one component.

Script: Fig 1B.py

Hexbin density scatter correlating RNA-seq log2 fold-change between the SSRP1 and SUPT16H knockdowns, for genes significantly changed in at least one condition.

Script: Fig 1C.py

Hexbin density scatter correlating ATAC-seq log2 fold-change between the SUPT16H and SSRP1 knockdowns, for peaks significantly differential in at least one condition.

Script: Fig 1D.py

ChIP-seq IP − INPUT average profile around TSS on an independent mouse (mm10) dataset.

Script: Fig 1E.py

docs.title: Figure 2 — ChIP-seq Heatmaps Split by RNA-seq Status
docs.text:
Pipeline: IntegratedHeatmapPipeline

Loads SSRP1 (2A) / SUPT16H (2B) ChIP-seq signal, synchronises it with RNA-seq results, and produces an integrated heatmap + profile with genes overlaid by RNA up/down/unchanged status. No category filtering — all genes are included.

2A — SSRP12B — SUPT16H

Script: Fig 2.py

docs.title: Figure 3 — CSV-only Decile Analysis (ChIP vs. RNA)
docs.text:
Pipeline: DecileScatterPipeline

Works entirely from a pre-merged CSV/TSV. Sorts genes by SSRP1 ChIP log2 fold-change into deciles and plots the corresponding RNA-seq log2 fold-change (SSRP1 in 3A, SUPT16H in 3B) as a dual-axis boxplot + stripplot, with no category filtering.

3A — SSRP1 RNA3B — SUPT16H RNA

Script: Fig 3.py

docs.title: Figure 4 — ChIP-seq Signal vs. ATAC-seq Status and Overlay
docs.text:
Pipelines: IntegratedHeatmapPipeline, OverlayProfilePipeline

4A/4B integrate SSRP1 and SUPT16H ChIP-seq signal with ATAC-seq up/down/unchanged status (profile overlay only, heatmaps hidden). 4C overlays SSRP1 ChIP-seq against its own ATAC-seq track on twin y-axes, with the CONTROL ATAC-seq track shown for reference.

4A — SSRP1 vs ATAC status4B — SUPT16H vs ATAC status4C — SSRP1 ChIP/ATAC overlay4D — SUPT16H ChIP/ATAC overlay

Script: Fig 4AB.py (4A/4B) · Fig 4CD.py (4C/4D)

docs.title: Figure 5 — ChIP-seq Heatmaps vs. RNA-seq Status, FACT-filtered
docs.text:
Pipeline: IntegratedHeatmapPipeline

Same as Figure 2, but restricted to genes classified as FACT high or low for the corresponding component (SSRP1 FACT category for 5A, SUPT16H FACT category for 5B).

5A — SSRP15B — SUPT16H

Script: Fig 5.py

docs.title: Figure 6 — RNA Violin Panels
docs.text:
Pipeline: RNAViolinPipeline

Draws four horizontal violin panels of RNA-seq log2 fold-change (SSRP1/SUPT16H × FACT high/low) with significant genes (padj < 0.1) overlaid as points, all in one figure with no subplot divisions.

Script: Fig 6.py

docs.title: Figure 7 — CSV-only Decile Analysis (ChIP vs. RNA), FACT-filtered
docs.text:
Pipeline: DecileScatterPipeline

Same as Figure 3, split into FACT high/low panels for both SSRP1 (7A/7B) and SUPT16H (7C/7D).

7A — SSRP1 FACT high7B — SSRP1 FACT low7C — SUPT16H FACT high7D — SUPT16H FACT low

Script: Fig 7.py

docs.title: Figure 8 — ChIP-seq Signal vs. ATAC-seq Status, FACT-filtered
docs.text:
Pipeline: IntegratedHeatmapPipeline

Same as Figure 4A/4B, but restricted to genes classified as FACT high or low for the corresponding component.

8A — SSRP18B — SUPT16H

Script: Fig 8.py

docs.title: Figure 9 — ATAC-seq Category Heatmaps
docs.text:
Pipeline: CategoryHeatmapPipeline

Loads the CONTROL, SSRP1 and SUPT16H ATAC-seq tracks and splits each into FACT high/low heatmaps (mean-sorted panel shown).

9A — CONTROL9B — SSRP19C — SUPT16H

Script: Fig 9.py

docs.title: Figure 10 — Volcano Plots
docs.text:
Pipeline: VolcanoPipeline

Volcano plots of ChIP-seq differential binding for SSRP1 (10A) and SUPT16H (10B), with a fixed gene highlight list (SERPINE1, F3, CYR61, TERT, RPSAP52, NEAT1) and no threshold-based auto-labeling.

10A — SSRP1 ChIP volcano10B — SUPT16H ChIP volcano

Script: Fig 10.py

docs.title: Figures 11–12 — Circos Plots Comparing Multi-signal Changes (-log10 padj)
docs.text:
Pipeline: CircPlotPipeline

Generates a circos plot per condition (SSRP1 → Figure 11, SUPT16H → Figure 12) comparing ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq -log10(padj) (via value_transform/value_label) for a configurable gene list (defaults to SERPINE1, F3, CYR61, TERT, RPSAP52, NEAT1), with a threshold of 0.1 suited to the transformed scale. Three concentric rings represent the three signal types, with connecting ribbons colored by magnitude. Gene data can optionally be exported to TSV alongside the figure.

11 — SSRP112 — SUPT16H

Script: Fig 11-12.py

docs.title: Figures 13–14 — Circos Plots Comparing Multi-signal Changes (log2FC)
docs.text:
Pipeline: CircPlotPipeline

Same gene list and layout as Figures 11–12, but plots log2 fold-change instead of -log10(padj) for each signal. SSRP1 → Figure 13, SUPT16H → Figure 14.

13 — SSRP114 — SUPT16H

Script: Fig 13-14.py

docs.title: Supplementary Figure 1 — Decile Analysis (ChIP vs. ATAC) and Quadrant Profiles
docs.text:
Pipelines: DecileScatterPipeline, GeneGroupProfilePipeline

S1A/S1B repeat the Figure 3 decile analysis using ATAC-seq log2 fold-change instead of RNA-seq (SSRP1 / SUPT16H, unfiltered). S1C/S1D classify genes into four ATAC×RNA log2FC quadrants (threshold ±1.0) and plot the average ChIP-seq TSS profile per quadrant.

S1A — SSRP1 ATAC decilesS1B — SUPT16H ATAC decilesS1C — SSRP1 quadrant profileS1D — SUPT16H quadrant profile

Script: Fig S1AB.py (S1A/S1B) · Fig S1CD.py (S1C/S1D)

docs.title: Supplementary Figure 2 — ChIP/ATAC Overlay Profiles, FACT-filtered
docs.text:
Pipeline: OverlayProfilePipeline

Dual-axis ChIP-seq vs. ATAC-seq overlay profiles (with the CONTROL ATAC-seq track shown for reference), split by FACT high/low for both SSRP1 (S2A/S2B) and SUPT16H (S2C/S2D).

S2A — SSRP1 FACT highS2B — SSRP1 FACT lowS2C — SUPT16H FACT highS2D — SUPT16H FACT low

Script: Fig S2.py

docs.title: Extra — Multi-signal Comparison (3-way Scatter)
docs.text:
Pipeline: MultiSignalComparisonPipeline

Compares log2 fold-change values across ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq and RNA-seq from a single expression-results CSV and produces a 1×3 panel of 2D scatter plots (RNA vs. ChIP, RNA vs. ATAC, ChIP vs. ATAC). Kept in examples/extra/ as a standalone reference, saved by default; set OUTPUT_PATH to None to skip saving.

Script: extra/multisignal_comparison.py

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Install Pyntegrate — see Installation
  2. Have the data files available:
    • A gffutils FeatureDB (.db file)
    • Signal files (.bw, .bam, .bed, ...)
    • CSV/TSV tables with gene annotations and expression results

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Script filenames contain spaces, so quote them:

cd examples/

# Run Figure 1E (ChIP-seq IP vs INPUT profile)
python "Fig 1E.py"

# Run Figure 10 (volcano plots)
python "Fig 10.py"

# Run the CSV-only decile analysis (Figure 3)
python "Fig 3.py"

docs.title: Customizing Paths and Parameters
docs.text:
Edit the Configuration section at the top of each script to match your data locations and analysis parameters. For example, in Fig 1E.py:

DB_PATH = "/path/to/your/annotations.db"
IP_BW = "/path/to/your/ip_signal.bw"
INPUT_BW = "/path/to/your/input_signal.bw"
GENOME = "mm10"  # or "hg19"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Common issues

  1. Verify that all data file paths are correct and the files exist
  2. Check that the genome version matches your data
  3. Ensure dependencies (bedtools, HOMER if needed) are installed and on your PATH
  4. Check that your CSV/TSV files have the columns referenced by the pipeline
  5. For more detail, inspect the full error traceback

For additional help, visit GitHub Issues.

docs.title: Getting Started with Pyntegrate
docs.text:
This guide walks through the basic Pyntegrate workflow: pointing a pipeline at your files and getting back ready-to-save matplotlib figures.

Prefer runnable code?

Every pattern shown here also exists as a complete, runnable script in examples/ — see the Examples gallery.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text: The recommended entry point is the Pyntegrate.pipelines module: each pipeline class wraps loading, processing, and plotting for one analysis type into a single call. You instantiate a pipeline with file paths and parameters, then call .run() to get back one or more matplotlib.figure.Figure objects — no separate "loading" step is required, the pipeline reads the files itself.

docs.title: 1. ChIP-seq IP vs. INPUT (PeakHeatmapPipeline)
docs.text:
from Pyntegrate.pipelines import PeakHeatmapPipeline

pipeline = PeakHeatmapPipeline(
    db_path="/path/to/annotations.gtf.db",  # gffutils FeatureDB
    ip_path="/path/to/ip_signal.bw",
    input_path="/path/to/input_signal.bw",
    genome="mm10",
    ip_extension="bigwig",
    input_extension="bigwig",
    bins=100,
    window=(-1000, 1000),
)
figs = pipeline.run()  # dict of Figures
figs["profile"].savefig("profile.png", dpi=300)
figs["heatmap_sorted_mean"].savefig("heatmap.png", dpi=300)
Parameter Description db_path Path to a gffutils FeatureDB (.db file) built from a GTF/GFF ip_path / input_path Path to the IP / INPUT signal file (BigWig, BAM, BED, ...) genome Reference genome (e.g. "hg19", "mm10") bins Number of signal bins across the TSS window window (upstream, downstream) bp around each TSS

Returns: a dict with keys "profile", "heatmap_no_sorted", "heatmap_sorted_mean", "heatmap_sorted_max".

docs.title: 2. Loading RNA-seq Data
docs.text:
The signal-based pipelines above take a signal file directly. Pipelines that integrate RNA-seq (or ATAC-seq) results take a CSV/TSV path directly too — no separate loading step needed, as shown in the next section. Pyntegrate.results_table also provides a lower-level DEseq2Results object model, useful if you want to filter/inspect a differential-expression table yourself before or instead of using a pipeline:

from Pyntegrate.results_table import DEseq2Results

rna = DEseq2Results(
    "/path/to/rna-seq.csv",
    id_column="GeneID",
    pval_column="padj",
    lfc_column="log2FoldChange",
    mean_column="baseMean",
)
up = rna.upregulated(thresh=0.05, idx=False)   # subsetted DEseq2Results

The CSV should contain at least a gene-ID column plus log2FoldChange and padj (or equivalently named columns you pass to lfc_column/pval_column).

docs.title: 3. Creating Visualizations
docs.text:
Signal integrated with RNA-seq statusVolcano Plot 
from Pyntegrate.pipelines import IntegratedHeatmapPipeline

pipeline = IntegratedHeatmapPipeline(
    db_path="/path/to/annotations.gtf.db",
    signal_path="/path/to/chip_signal.bw",
    expression_table_path="/path/to/rna-seq.csv",
    genome="hg19",
    gene_id_col="GeneID",
    lfc_col="log2FoldChange",
    divided_by="RNA",
    threshold=1.0,
    signal_name="ChIP-seq",
)
fig = pipeline.run()
fig.savefig("integrated_output.png", dpi=300)

from Pyntegrate.pipelines import VolcanoPipeline

pipeline = VolcanoPipeline(
    csv_path="/path/to/rna-seq.csv",
    gene_id_col="GeneID",
    padj_col="padj",
    lfc_col="log2FoldChange",
)
fig = pipeline.run()
fig.savefig("volcano.png", dpi=300)

Every pipeline follows this same shape: construct it with paths/parameters, call .run(), then .savefig(...) on whatever it returns (a single Figure, or a dict/tuple of them — see each pipeline's docstring in the API reference for its exact return type).

docs.title: Supported Signal Files
docs.text:
Format Notes BigWig (.bw) Recommended for large-scale, pre-computed signal data BAM (.bam) Aligned reads; signal is computed on the fly BED (.bed) Genomic intervals

Pass the matching type via *_extension="bigwig" / "bam" / "bed" on the pipeline.

docs.title: Supported Feature Files
docs.text: Format Notes GTF / GFF Gene annotations — pre-built into a gffutils .db file, passed as db_path BED Genomic intervals, e.g. for GeneScaleRegionsProfilePipeline

docs.title: RNA-seq / ATAC-seq Table Format
docs.text:
A CSV or TSV with at least:

Column Description A gene/peak ID column Passed as gene_id_col (or similar) — must match IDs in db_path A log2 fold-change column Passed as lfc_col An adjusted p-value column Passed as padj_col (where applicable)

docs.title: Example: Complete Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
from Pyntegrate.pipelines import IntegratedHeatmapPipeline

pipeline = IntegratedHeatmapPipeline(
    db_path="genes.gtf.db",
    signal_path="chipseq.bw",
    expression_table_path="rna_data.csv",
    genome="hg38",
    gene_id_col="GeneID",
    lfc_col="log2FoldChange",
    divided_by="RNA",
    bins=100,
    threshold=1.0,
    signal_name="ChIP-seq",
)

fig = pipeline.run()
fig.savefig("analysis_output.png", dpi=300)

docs.title: Filter by Category (e.g. FACT high/low)
docs.text:
Most pipelines accept category_table_path + category_col + categories to subset genes by a label column in a CSV, rather than requiring you to pre-filter the signal yourself:

pipeline = IntegratedHeatmapPipeline(
    db_path="genes.gtf.db",
    signal_path="chipseq.bw",
    expression_table_path="rna_data.csv",
    genome="hg38",
    gene_id_col="GeneID",
    lfc_col="log2FoldChange",
    divided_by="RNA",
    category_table_path="fact_categories.csv",
    category_col="fact_category",
    categories=["high", "low"],
)

docs.title: Create Higher-Resolution Heatmaps
docs.text:
Increase the bins parameter for finer resolution:

pipeline = PeakHeatmapPipeline(
    db_path="genes.gtf.db",
    ip_path="chipseq.bw",
    input_path="input.bw",
    genome="hg38",
    bins=200,  # higher resolution than the default 100
)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Pyntegrate works best inside an isolated Conda environment. Before installing, make sure you have:

Requirement Why Python 3.9-3.12 numpy 1.26 and pybedtools 0.9.1 do not build on Python 3.13+ (3.10 recommended) conda Manages the Python environment and native dependencies (e.g. bedtools) Git Needed to clone the repository or install directly from GitHub C/C++ build toolchain Required to compile some scientific-Python dependencies pip Installs Pyntegrate and its Python dependencies inside the environment LinuxmacOS

Install the basic system tools first:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git build-essential

Install the Apple command line tools:

xcode-select --install

docs.title: Quick Installation
docs.text:
Pick the workflow that matches your setup. The setup script is the fastest path — it creates the environment, installs Pyntegrate, and takes care of bedtools for you in one command.

One-command script Conda (manual)

The repository ships a helper script that creates a venv, installs Pyntegrate in editable mode from a local clone, and installs bedtools automatically (via conda, apt-get, or brew, whichever is available) — handy for development or for running the examples/ scripts:

git clone https://github.com/Molecular-Oncology-Group-UFV/Pyntegrate.git
cd Pyntegrate
./setup_env.sh          # creates .venv/, installs Pyntegrate + bedtools
# ./setup_env.sh /path/to/venv   # optional: custom venv location
# PYTHON=/usr/bin/python3.11 ./setup_env.sh   # optional: choose the interpreter

source .venv/bin/activate

Creates a clean environment and installs Pyntegrate in editable mode from a local clone. Conda installs only what pip cannot (bedtools, samtools, and pybedtools, which often fails to compile under pip); pip install -e . then installs the remaining Python dependencies at the versions pinned in requirements.txt:

conda create --name pyntegrate -c conda-forge -c bioconda \
    python=3.10 bedtools samtools pybedtools=0.9.1 -y
conda activate pyntegrate

git clone https://github.com/Molecular-Oncology-Group-UFV/Pyntegrate.git
cd Pyntegrate
pip install -e .

Activate the environment you just created

Make sure the name passed to conda activate matches the one used in conda create. Otherwise everything is installed into a different (possibly older) environment.

docs.title: Install from a local copy
docs.text:
From a ZIP download 
conda create --name pyntegrate -c conda-forge -c bioconda \
    python=3.10 bedtools samtools pybedtools=0.9.1 -y
conda activate pyntegrate

unzip Pyntegrate-main.zip
cd Pyntegrate-main
pip install .

Editable install for development

If you plan to modify Pyntegrate or run the examples/ scripts against a local checkout, install in editable mode instead: pip install -e .

docs.title: HOMER
docs.text:
HOMER is optional and only needed for functions related to peak annotation and enrichment analysis.

Follow the HOMER installation instructions for your system.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
After installation, check from the terminal (with the environment activated) that the package imports correctly:

python -c "import Pyntegrate; print(Pyntegrate.__version__)"

If the import succeeds, the installation is ready. You can also confirm that bedtools is available:

which bedtools
bedtools --version

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Conda solver errors (excluded by strict repo priority, unsatisfiable packages)

conda-forge must take priority over bioconda. Check the order with conda config --show channels; conda-forge should be listed first. To fix it:

conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge   # the last one added goes on top

Avoid conda install-ing packages that pip install -e . already installs (e.g. numpy, pandas, pycirclize): pip will replace them with the versions pinned in requirements.txt, and mixing both can cause conflicts.

NumPy version conflicts

If you see an error related to NumPy, reinstall the version pinned by the project from inside the activated environment:

pip install --force-reinstall numpy==1.26.3
bedtools not found

If a function complains that bedtools is missing, verify that it is installed and available on your PATH:

which bedtools

If it is installed but not found, reactivate the Conda environment, or add the binary's location to PATH manually.

docs.title: Building the documentation locally
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme. Those tools are not part of Pyntegrate's runtime dependencies, so install them separately:

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt

mkdocs serve   # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build   # static site in site/

Ready to go? Continue to Getting Started.

docs.title: Array Helpers API
docs.text:
Array manipulation and processing utilities.

Low-level, format-agnostic helpers for extracting genomic signal into NumPy arrays.

These functions power the public API in Pyntegrate._genomic_signal (BaseSignal.array, local_coverage, IntervalSignal.local_count, count_array, etc.) by doing the actual per-feature/per-window computation — they are not usually called directly by end users.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text: Function Description _local_count Count signal items (reads/intervals) within a single genomic interval. _local_coverage Compute a binned coverage vector for one or more genomic intervals. _array / _array_star / _array_parallel Build per-feature signal arrays, optionally distributed across multiple processes. _count_array / _count_array_star / _count_array_parallel Build per-feature signal counts, optionally distributed across multiple processes. remove_duplicates Deduplicate gene_id entries in a GTF file, overwriting it in place.

docs.text:
Compute binned, aggregated peak values over a genomic interval.

Intersects self.bedtool with interval, then aggregates the narrowPeak signal value (column 7) of overlapping peaks into bins evenly-sized bins using function.

If None, uses the length of interval. function str "mean" Aggregation function: "mean", "sum", "min", or "max". zero_inf bool True If True, replace ±inf values with zero before returning. zero_nan bool True If True, replace NaN values with zero before returning.

Source code in Pyntegrate/filetype_adapters.py 
def summarize(self, interval, bins=None, function='mean', zero_inf=True, zero_nan=True):
    """
    Compute binned, aggregated peak values over a genomic interval.

    Intersects `self.bedtool` with `interval`, then aggregates the
    narrowPeak signal value (column 7) of overlapping peaks into
    `bins` evenly-sized bins using `function`.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `interval` | `object` | — | Object with `chrom` (`str`), `start` (`int`), and `stop` (`int`) attributes. |
    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins. If `None`, uses the length of `interval`. |
    | `function` | `str` | `"mean"` | Aggregation function: `"mean"`, `"sum"`, `"min"`, or `"max"`. |
    | `zero_inf` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `±inf` values with zero before returning. |
    | `zero_nan` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `NaN` values with zero before returning. |

    ## Returns

    `np.ndarray` — Array of shape `(bins,)` with the aggregated
    signal value per bin.
    """
    # Set bins to interval length if not specified
    # Ensure the BedTool object is ready
    self.make_fileobj()

    # Rest of the summarize function implementation...
    if bins is None:
        bins = interval.stop - interval.start

    s = np.zeros((bins,))
    seen = np.zeros((bins,), dtype=bool)
    bin_size = (interval.stop - interval.start) / bins
    bin_edges = np.linspace(interval.start, interval.stop, bins + 1)

    query_interval = pybedtools.BedTool(
        [pybedtools.Interval(interval.chrom, interval.start, interval.stop)]
    )
    overlapping_intervals = self.bedtool.intersect(query_interval, wa=True)

    for peak in overlapping_intervals:
        peak_start = max(interval.start, peak.start)
        peak_end = min(interval.stop, peak.end)

        bin_start_idx = int((peak_start - interval.start) // bin_size)
        bin_end_idx = min(int((peak_end - interval.start) // bin_size), bins - 1)

        for i in range(bin_start_idx, bin_end_idx + 1):
            bin_start = bin_edges[i]
            bin_end = bin_edges[i + 1]
            overlap_start = max(peak_start, bin_start)
            overlap_end = min(peak_end, bin_end)
            overlap_length = overlap_end - overlap_start

            if overlap_length > 0:
                if function == 'mean':
                    s[i] += float(peak[6]) * overlap_length / bin_size
                elif function == 'sum':
                    s[i] += float(peak[6])
                elif function == 'min':
                    if not seen[i]:
                        s[i] = float(peak[6])
                        seen[i] = True
                    else:
                        s[i] = min(s[i], float(peak[6]))
                elif function == 'max':
                    if not seen[i]:
                        s[i] = float(peak[6])
                        seen[i] = True
                    else:
                        s[i] = max(s[i], float(peak[6]))

    if zero_nan:
        s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
    if zero_inf:
        s[np.isinf(s)] = 0

    return s

def summarize(self, interval, bins=None, method='summarize',
              function='mean', zero_inf=True, zero_nan=True):
    """
    Compute binned, aggregated bigWig values over a genomic interval.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `interval` | `object` | — | Object with `chrom` (`str`), `start` (`int`), and `stop` (`int`) attributes. |
    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins. If `None`, uses the length of `interval`. |
    | `method` | `str` | `"summarize"` | `"summarize"` and `"get_as_array"` use bx-python; `"ucsc_summarize"` uses `bigWigSummary`. See `Pyntegrate.array_helpers._local_coverage` for further notes. `None` is treated as `"summarize"`. |
    | `function` | `str` | `"mean"` | Aggregation function: `"mean"`, `"sum"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"std"`, or `"coverage"`. Ignored when `method="get_as_array"`; `"coverage"` is only valid with `method="ucsc_summarize"`. |
    | `zero_inf` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `±inf` values with zero before returning. |
    | `zero_nan` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `NaN` values with zero before returning. |

    ## Returns

    `np.ndarray` — Aggregated signal values, one per bin.

    ## Raises

    `ValueError` — If `function` is not supported by the chosen
    `method`, or if `method` is not one of `"summarize"`,
    `"ucsc_summarize"`, or `"get_as_array"`.
    """

    if method is None:
        method = 'summarize'

    # We may be dividing by zero in some cases, which raises a warning in
    # NumPy based on the IEEE 754 standard (see
    # http://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/
    #       numpy.seterr.html)
    #
    # That's OK -- we're expecting that to happen sometimes. So temporarily
    # disable this error reporting for the duration of this method.
    orig = np.geterr()['invalid']
    np.seterr(invalid='ignore')

    if (bins is None) or (method == 'get_as_array'):
        bw = self.fileobj
        chrom = interval.chrom
        if isinstance(chrom, str):
            chrom = chrom.encode()
        s = bw.get_as_array(
            chrom,
            interval.start,
            interval.stop,)
        if s is None:
            s = np.zeros((interval.stop - interval.start,))
        else:
            if zero_nan:
                s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
            if zero_inf:
                s[np.isinf(s)] = 0

    elif method == 'ucsc_summarize':
        if function in ['mean', 'min', 'max', 'std', 'coverage']:
            return self.ucsc_summarize(interval, bins, function=function)
        else:
            raise ValueError('function "%s" not supported by UCSC\'s'
                             'bigWigSummary')

    elif method == 'summarize':
        bw = self.fileobj
        s = bw.summarize(
            interval.chrom,
            interval.start,
            interval.stop, bins)

        if s is None:
            s = np.zeros((bins,))
        else:
            if function == 'sum':
                s = s.sum_data
            elif function == 'mean':
                s = s.sum_data / s.valid_count
                if zero_nan:
                    s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
            elif function == 'min':
                s = s.min_val
                if zero_inf:
                    s[np.isinf(s)] = 0
            elif function == 'max':
                s = s.max_val
                if zero_inf:
                    s[np.isinf(s)] = 0
            elif function == 'std':
                s = (s.sum_squares / s.valid_count)
                if zero_nan:
                    s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
            else:
                raise ValueError(
                        'function "%s" not supported by bx-python'
                        % function
                )

    else:
        raise ValueError("method '%s' not in [summarize, ucsc_summarize, get_as_array]" % method)

    # Reset NumPy error reporting
    np.seterr(divide=orig)
    return s

def ucsc_summarize(self, interval, bins=None, function='mean'):
    """
    Summarize a bigWig interval by shelling out to UCSC's `bigWigSummary`.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `interval` | `object` | — | Object with `chrom` (`str`), `start` (`int`), and `stop` (`int`) attributes. |
    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins. If `None`, uses `len(interval)`. |
    | `function` | `str` | `"mean"` | Aggregation type passed to `bigWigSummary -type=`, e.g. `"mean"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"std"`, or `"coverage"`. |

    ## Returns

    `np.ndarray` — Array of shape `(bins,)` with the summarized
    value per bin. Bins with no data from `bigWigSummary` remain `0`.

    ## Raises

    `ValueError` — If the `bigWigSummary` subprocess exits with a
    non-zero, non-`None` return code (other than the "no data" case).
    """
    if bins is None:
        bins = len(interval)
    y = np.zeros(bins)
    cmds = [
        'bigWigSummary',
        self.fn,
        interval.chrom,
        str(interval.start),
        str(interval.stop),
        str(bins),
        '-type=%s' % function]
    p = subprocess.Popen(
        cmds,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
    )

    def gen():
        try:
            for line in p.stdout:
                yield line
        finally:
            if p.poll() is None:
                return
            else:
                p.wait()
                err = p.stderr.read().strip()
                if p.returncode not in (0, None):
                    if err.startswith('no data'):
                        return
                    raise ValueError(
                        "cmds: %s: %s" %
                        (' '.join(cmds), p.stderr.read()))
                if len(err) != 0:
                    sys.stderr.write(err)

    for line in gen():
        for i, x in enumerate(line.split('\t')):
            try:
                y[i] = float(x)
            except ValueError:
                pass
    return np.array(y)

docs.title: rebin(x, y, nbin)
docs.text:
Linearly interpolate y onto a new uniform grid of nbin points.

Constructs a new x-axis of nbin evenly-spaced points spanning [x.min(), x.max()], then uses linear interpolation to evaluate y at each new point. Useful for normalising genomic signal profiles so that regions of different lengths can be compared or averaged.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description x np.ndarray — Original x-axis coordinates, shape (N,). y np.ndarray — Original y-axis values, shape (N,). nbin int — Number of evenly-spaced points in the output grid.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] — (xi, yi) where xi is the new x-axis of shape (nbin,) and yi contains the interpolated y values at each point of xi, also shape (nbin,).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from Pyntegrate.helpers import rebin

x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.5])
xi, yi = rebin(x, y, nbin=3)
print(xi)
print(np.round(yi, 4))

Output: 

[0. 2. 4.]
[0.   0.5  1.5]

def rebin(x, y, nbin):
    """
    Linearly interpolate `y` onto a new uniform grid of `nbin` points.

    Constructs a new x-axis of `nbin` evenly-spaced points spanning
    `[x.min(), x.max()]`, then uses linear interpolation to evaluate
    `y` at each new point. Useful for normalising genomic signal
    profiles so that regions of different lengths can be compared or
    averaged.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `x` | `np.ndarray` | — | Original x-axis coordinates, shape `(N,)`. |
    | `y` | `np.ndarray` | — | Original y-axis values, shape `(N,)`. |
    | `nbin` | `int` | — | Number of evenly-spaced points in the output grid. |

    ## Returns

    `tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]` — `(xi, yi)` where `xi` is the new
    x-axis of shape `(nbin,)` and `yi` contains the interpolated y
    values at each point of `xi`, also shape `(nbin,)`.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import rebin

    x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
    y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.5])
    xi, yi = rebin(x, y, nbin=3)
    print(xi)
    print(np.round(yi, 4))
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    [0. 2. 4.]
    [0.   0.5  1.5]
    ```
    """
    xi = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), nbin)
    return xi, np.interp(xi, x, y)

The last chunk may contain fewer than n elements if the total length of f is not a multiple of n. This is used internally to distribute genomic features across parallel worker processes.

Output:

Source code in Pyntegrate/helpers.py 
def chunker(f, n):
    """
    Split an iterable into successive chunks of at most `n` elements.

    The last chunk may contain fewer than `n` elements if the total
    length of `f` is not a multiple of `n`. This is used internally
    to distribute genomic features across parallel worker processes.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `f` | `iterable` | — | Any iterable to be split into chunks. |
    | `n` | `int` | — | Maximum number of elements per chunk. |

    ## Yields

    `tuple` — Successive tuples of at most `n` elements drawn from `f`.
    The last tuple may be shorter.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import chunker

    result = list(chunker(range(7), 3))
    print(result)
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    [(0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6,)]
    ```
    """
    f = iter(f)
    x = []
    while 1:
        if len(x) < n:
            try:
                x.append(f.__next__())
            except StopIteration:
                if len(x) > 0:
                    yield tuple(x)
                break
        else:
            yield tuple(x)
            x = []

def list_example_files(pattern=None, full_path=False):
    """
    List example data files bundled with Pyntegrate.

    Scans the internal `test/data/` directory and optionally filters
    results by a glob pattern.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `pattern` | `str \| None` | `None` | Glob pattern to filter filenames (e.g. `"*.bigwig"`). If `None`, all files in the data directory are listed. |
    | `full_path` | `bool` | `False` | If `True`, return absolute paths. If `False`, return bare filenames only. |

    ## Returns

    `list[str]` — List of matching filenames or full paths.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import list_example_files

    # All example files (basenames only)
    print(list_example_files())
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    ['gdc.bam', 'gdc.bam.bai', 'gdc.bed', 'gdc.bigwig', ...]
    ```

    ```python
    # Only BigWig files, with full paths
    print(list_example_files("*.bigwig", full_path=True))
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    ['/path/to/Pyntegrate/test/data/gdc.bigwig', ...]
    ```
    """
    if not os.path.isdir(data_dir()):
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"Example data directory not found: {data_dir()}. "
            "The bundled metaseq example dataset is not included in this "
            "installation of Pyntegrate."
        )
    if pattern is None:
        files = os.listdir(data_dir())
    else:
        files = glob.glob(os.path.join(data_dir(), pattern))
    if full_path:
        return files
    else:
        return [os.path.basename(i) for i in files]

def split_feature(f, n):
    """
    Split a genomic interval into `n` roughly equal sub-intervals.

    Divides the feature by stepping through it in increments of
    `(stop - start) / n` base pairs. The last sub-interval is
    clipped to the original stop coordinate.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `f` | `pybedtools.Interval` | — | Genomic interval to split. All attributes (chrom, name, strand, etc.) are copied to each piece. |
    | `n` | `int` | — | Number of sub-intervals to create. |

    ## Yields

    `pybedtools.Interval` — Sub-intervals of `f` with adjusted `start`
    and `stop` coordinates and all other attributes preserved.

    ## Raises

    `ValueError` — If `n` is not an integer.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import pybedtools
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import split_feature

    feature = pybedtools.create_interval_from_list(
        ["chr1", "1000", "2000", "gene1", ".", "+"]
    )
    for piece in split_feature(feature, n=3):
        print(piece.chrom, piece.start, piece.stop)
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    chr1 1000 1333
    chr1 1333 1667
    chr1 1667 2000
    ```
    """
    if not isinstance(n, int):
        raise ValueError('n must be an integer')
    orig_feature = copy(f)
    breakpoints = [
        int(round(orig_feature.start + i * (orig_feature.stop - orig_feature.start) / n))
        for i in range(n + 1)
    ]
    for i in range(n):
        piece = copy(orig_feature)
        piece.start = breakpoints[i]
        piece.stop = breakpoints[i + 1]
        yield piece

def tointerval(s):
    """
    Convert a coordinate string to a `pybedtools.Interval`.

    Pass-through for anything that is already an interval-like object.

    Accepted string formats:

    - `"chrom:start-stop"` — e.g. `"chr1:1000-2000"`
    - `"chrom:start-stop[strand]"` — e.g. `"chr1:1000-2000[+]"`

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `s` | `str \| interval-like` | — | Coordinate string or an existing interval object. Non-string values are returned unchanged. |

    ## Returns

    `pybedtools.Interval` — Parsed interval, or `s` unchanged if it is
    not a string.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import tointerval

    iv = tointerval("chr1:1000-2000")
    print(iv.chrom, iv.start, iv.stop)

    iv_stranded = tointerval("chrX:500-1500[+]")
    print(iv_stranded.chrom, iv_stranded.start, iv_stranded.stop, iv_stranded.strand)
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    chr1 1000 2000
    chrX 500 1500 +
    ```
    """
    if isinstance(s, str):
        m = coord_re.search(s)
        if m.group('strand'):
            return pybedtools.create_interval_from_list([
                m.group('chrom'),
                m.group('start'),
                m.group('stop'),
                '.',
                '0',
                m.group('strand')])
        else:
            return pybedtools.create_interval_from_list([
                m.group('chrom'),
                m.group('start'),
                m.group('stop'),
            ])
    return s

def map_color(a, down_log2FoldChange, upper_log2FoldChange, upper_nlog10):
    """
    Classify a gene into an expression-change category for volcano-plot colouring.

    Returns one of three string labels based on whether the gene's
    log2 fold-change and transformed p-value exceed the given thresholds.
    Used internally by volcano-plot functions to assign point colours.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `a` | `tuple[float, float]` | — | A `(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj))` pair for a single gene. |
    | `down_log2FoldChange` | `float` | — | LFC threshold for down-regulation (typically negative, e.g. `-1.5`). |
    | `upper_log2FoldChange` | `float` | — | LFC threshold for up-regulation (e.g. `1.5`). |
    | `upper_nlog10` | `float` | — | `-log10(padj)` threshold for statistical significance. |

    ## Returns

    `str` — One of `"increase"`, `"decrease"`, or `"not significant"`.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import map_color

    print(map_color((2.0, 5.0), -1.5, 1.5, 2.0))
    print(map_color((-2.5, 4.0), -1.5, 1.5, 2.0))
    print(map_color((0.5, 1.0), -1.5, 1.5, 2.0))
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    increase
    decrease
    not significant
    ```
    """
    log2FoldChange, nlog10 = a

    if log2FoldChange > upper_log2FoldChange and nlog10 > upper_nlog10:
        return 'increase'
    elif log2FoldChange < down_log2FoldChange and nlog10 > upper_nlog10:
        return 'decrease'
    return 'not significant'

def remove_duplicates(fileName):
    """
    Remove duplicate gene entries from a GTF file, overwriting it in-place.

    Reads the file line-by-line, keeps the first occurrence of each
    unique `gene_id` (Ensembl version suffix stripped), and writes the
    result back to the same path. Lines whose `gene_id` cannot be
    parsed are silently dropped.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `fileName` | `str` | — | Path to the GTF file. **The file is overwritten.** |

    ## Returns

    `None`

    ## Notes

    Deduplication key is the `gene_id` attribute after stripping the
    Ensembl version suffix (e.g. `ENSG000001.3` → `ENSG000001`).

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate.array_helpers import remove_duplicates

    # Deduplicate a GTF before building a gffutils database
    remove_duplicates("gencode.v44.annotation.gtf")
    ```
    """
    seen_gene_ids = set()
    output_lines = []

    with open(fileName, 'r') as f_in:
        for line in f_in:
            fields = line.strip().split('\t')

            attributes = fields[-1]
            gene_id = None

            if 'gene_id "' in attributes:
                try:
                    gene_id = attributes.split('gene_id "')[1].split('"; ')[0]
                    gene_id = gene_id.split('.')[0]
                except IndexError:
                    gene_id = None

            if gene_id:
                if gene_id not in seen_gene_ids:
                    seen_gene_ids.add(gene_id)
                    output_lines.append(line)

    with open(fileName, 'w') as f_out:
        f_out.writelines(output_lines)

Tools for adjusting and customizing colormaps for visualizations.

Custom colormap utilities for genomic signal visualisation.

Provides helpers for creating diverging colormaps centred on zero, power-law adjustments, and centre-point shifting. The main utility is smart_colormap, which automatically matches colour saturation between the positive and negative halves of asymmetric data ranges.

Build a diverging colormap centred on zero for asymmetric data.

Creates a white-centred, three-stop colormap where the saturation and value of the "low" colour mirror those of color_high at the symmetric counterpart, then the hue is shifted to hue_low. This ensures that colours at equal distance from zero appear equally vivid even when |vmin| ≠ |vmax|.

def smart_colormap(vmin, vmax, color_high='#b11902', hue_low=0.6):
    """
    Build a diverging colormap centred on zero for asymmetric data.

    Creates a white-centred, three-stop colormap where the saturation
    and value of the "low" colour mirror those of `color_high` at the
    symmetric counterpart, then the hue is shifted to `hue_low`. This
    ensures that colours at equal distance from zero appear equally
    vivid even when `|vmin| ≠ |vmax|`.

    If both extremes are effectively zero the function returns the
    string `"Greys"` as a safe fallback.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `vmin` | `float` | — | Minimum value in the data to be plotted. |
    | `vmax` | `float` | — | Maximum value in the data to be plotted. |
    | `color_high` | `str` | `"#b11902"` | Matplotlib colour for the high (positive) end of the scale. |
    | `hue_low` | `float` | `0.6` | HSV hue `[0, 1]` for the low (negative) end. `0.6` gives a muted blue. |

    ## Returns

    `matplotlib.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap | str` — A 2048-colour
    diverging colormap, or `"Greys"` when both extremes are zero.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from Pyntegrate.colormap_adjust import smart_colormap

    cmap = smart_colormap(vmin=-3, vmax=9)
    data = np.random.uniform(-3, 9, (50, 50))

    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    im = ax.imshow(data, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto", vmin=-3, vmax=9)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
    plt.title("Asymmetric diverging colormap")
    plt.show()
    ```
    """
    orig_cmap = matplotlib.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
        'test', ['#FFFFFF', color_high], N=2048)

    vmin = float(vmin)
    vmax = float(vmax)
    mx = max([vmin, vmax])
    mn = min([vmin, vmax])
    if mx == 0 or mn == 0 or np.isclose(mx, 0):
        return "Greys"

    frac = abs(mn / mx)

    rgb = orig_cmap(frac)[:-1]

    hsv = list(colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(*rgb))
    hsv[0] = hue_low
    new_rgb = colorsys.hsv_to_rgb(*hsv)

    zeropoint = abs(-vmin / (vmax - vmin))

    new_cmap = matplotlib.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
        'test', [(0, new_rgb), (zeropoint, '#FFFFFF'), (1, color_high)],
        N=2048)

    return new_cmap

def cmap_powerlaw_adjust(cmap, a):
    """
    Rescale colormap indices via a power-law transformation.

    Applies `new_index = old_index ** a` to the colour lookup table,
    compressing or expanding whichever end of the colormap has the most
    visual resolution. Values `a < 0` return the input unchanged.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `cmap` | `matplotlib.colors.Colormap` | — | Input colormap instance (e.g. `cm.jet`). |
    | `a` | `float` | — | Power-law exponent. `a > 1` compresses the low end; `a < 1` compresses the high end. `a < 0` returns the input unchanged. |

    ## Returns

    `matplotlib.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap` — A new 1024-colour
    colormap with power-law adjusted index positions.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import matplotlib.cm as cm
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import numpy as np
    from Pyntegrate.colormap_adjust import cmap_powerlaw_adjust

    data = np.random.exponential(scale=1.0, size=(40, 40))
    adjusted = cmap_powerlaw_adjust(cm.viridis, a=0.5)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3))
    axes[0].imshow(data, cmap=cm.viridis)
    axes[0].set_title("Original")
    axes[1].imshow(data, cmap=adjusted)
    axes[1].set_title("Power-law adjusted (a=0.5)")
    plt.show()
    ```
    """
    if a < 0.:
        return cmap
    cdict = copy.copy(cmap._segmentdata)
    fn = lambda x: (x[0] ** a, x[1], x[2])
    for key in ('red', 'green', 'blue'):
        cdict[key] = list(map(fn, cdict[key]))
        cdict[key].sort()
        assert (cdict[key][0][0] >= 0 and cdict[key][-1][0] <= 1), \
            "Resulting indices extend out of the [0, 1] segment."
    return colors.LinearSegmentedColormap('colormap', cdict, 1024)

def cmap_center_adjust(cmap, center_ratio):
    """
    Shift the perceptual midpoint of a colormap to a new relative position.

    Converts `center_ratio` to a power-law exponent via a log
    transform and delegates to
    [`cmap_powerlaw_adjust`][Pyntegrate.colormap_adjust.cmap_powerlaw_adjust].
    The colour that was previously at index 0.5 will now appear at
    `center_ratio`. Returns the input unchanged when `center_ratio`
    is outside `(0, 1)`.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `cmap` | `matplotlib.colors.Colormap` | — | Input colormap instance. |
    | `center_ratio` | `float` | — | New position of the old midpoint colour, in `(0, 1)`. `> 0.5` pulls the centre toward the high end; `< 0.5` toward the low end. |

    ## Returns

    `matplotlib.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap` — Adjusted colormap, or
    the input unchanged if `center_ratio` is not in `(0, 1)`.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import matplotlib.cm as cm
    from Pyntegrate.colormap_adjust import cmap_center_adjust

    # Pull the midpoint 25 % toward the high end
    adjusted = cmap_center_adjust(cm.seismic, center_ratio=0.75)
    ```
    """
    if not (0. < center_ratio) & (center_ratio < 1.):
        return cmap
    a = math.log(center_ratio) / math.log(0.5)
    return cmap_powerlaw_adjust(cmap, a)

def cmap_center_point_adjust(cmap, range, center):
    """
    Shift a colormap so that a specific data value maps to the midpoint colour.

    Converts the absolute `center` value to a fractional position
    within `range` and calls
    [`cmap_center_adjust`][Pyntegrate.colormap_adjust.cmap_center_adjust].
    Typical use: force zero (or another anchor) to map to white in a
    diverging colormap. Returns the input unchanged when `center` lies
    outside `range`.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `cmap` | `matplotlib.colors.Colormap` | — | Input colormap instance. |
    | `range` | `tuple[float, float]` | — | `(min, max)` of the data being plotted. |
    | `center` | `float` | — | Data value that should correspond to the colormap midpoint. Must satisfy `range[0] < center < range[1]`. |

    ## Returns

    `matplotlib.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap` — Adjusted colormap, or
    the input unchanged when `center` is outside `range`.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    import matplotlib.cm as cm
    from Pyntegrate.colormap_adjust import cmap_center_point_adjust

    # Force 0 to be white in a dataset ranging from -2 to +8
    cmap = cmap_center_point_adjust(cm.seismic, range=(-2, 8), center=0)

    data = np.random.uniform(-2, 8, (40, 40))
    plt.imshow(data, cmap=cmap, vmin=-2, vmax=8, aspect="auto")
    plt.colorbar()
    plt.title("Zero centred on white")
    plt.show()
    ```
    """
    if not ((range[0] < center) and (center < range[1])):
        return cmap
    return cmap_center_adjust(
        cmap,
        abs(center - range[0]) / abs(range[1] - range[0]))

docs.title: Genomic Signal API
docs.text:
Core genomic signal class for handling signal data.

Uniform interface for computing genomic signal from multiple file formats.

This module provides classes that wrap BAM, BigWig, BigBed, BED, and NarrowPeak files behind a single API, so that coverage and count arrays can be computed with one call regardless of the underlying file format.

If None, uses the length of interval. function str "mean" Aggregation function: "mean", "sum", "min", or "max". zero_inf bool True If True, replace ±inf values with zero before returning. zero_nan bool True If True, replace NaN values with zero before returning.

def summarize(self, interval, bins=None, function='mean', zero_inf=True, zero_nan=True):
    """
    Compute binned, aggregated peak values over a genomic interval.

    Intersects `self.bedtool` with `interval`, then aggregates the
    narrowPeak signal value (column 7) of overlapping peaks into
    `bins` evenly-sized bins using `function`.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `interval` | `object` | — | Object with `chrom` (`str`), `start` (`int`), and `stop` (`int`) attributes. |
    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins. If `None`, uses the length of `interval`. |
    | `function` | `str` | `"mean"` | Aggregation function: `"mean"`, `"sum"`, `"min"`, or `"max"`. |
    | `zero_inf` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `±inf` values with zero before returning. |
    | `zero_nan` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `NaN` values with zero before returning. |

    ## Returns

    `np.ndarray` — Array of shape `(bins,)` with the aggregated
    signal value per bin.
    """
    # Set bins to interval length if not specified
    # Ensure the BedTool object is ready
    self.make_fileobj()

    # Rest of the summarize function implementation...
    if bins is None:
        bins = interval.stop - interval.start

    s = np.zeros((bins,))
    seen = np.zeros((bins,), dtype=bool)
    bin_size = (interval.stop - interval.start) / bins
    bin_edges = np.linspace(interval.start, interval.stop, bins + 1)

    query_interval = pybedtools.BedTool(
        [pybedtools.Interval(interval.chrom, interval.start, interval.stop)]
    )
    overlapping_intervals = self.bedtool.intersect(query_interval, wa=True)

    for peak in overlapping_intervals:
        peak_start = max(interval.start, peak.start)
        peak_end = min(interval.stop, peak.end)

        bin_start_idx = int((peak_start - interval.start) // bin_size)
        bin_end_idx = min(int((peak_end - interval.start) // bin_size), bins - 1)

        for i in range(bin_start_idx, bin_end_idx + 1):
            bin_start = bin_edges[i]
            bin_end = bin_edges[i + 1]
            overlap_start = max(peak_start, bin_start)
            overlap_end = min(peak_end, bin_end)
            overlap_length = overlap_end - overlap_start

            if overlap_length > 0:
                if function == 'mean':
                    s[i] += float(peak[6]) * overlap_length / bin_size
                elif function == 'sum':
                    s[i] += float(peak[6])
                elif function == 'min':
                    if not seen[i]:
                        s[i] = float(peak[6])
                        seen[i] = True
                    else:
                        s[i] = min(s[i], float(peak[6]))
                elif function == 'max':
                    if not seen[i]:
                        s[i] = float(peak[6])
                        seen[i] = True
                    else:
                        s[i] = max(s[i], float(peak[6]))

    if zero_nan:
        s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
    if zero_inf:
        s[np.isinf(s)] = 0

    return s

    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins. If `None`, uses the length of `interval`. |
    | `method` | `str` | `"summarize"` | `"summarize"` and `"get_as_array"` use bx-python; `"ucsc_summarize"` uses `bigWigSummary`. See `Pyntegrate.array_helpers._local_coverage` for further notes. `None` is treated as `"summarize"`. |
    | `function` | `str` | `"mean"` | Aggregation function: `"mean"`, `"sum"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"std"`, or `"coverage"`. Ignored when `method="get_as_array"`; `"coverage"` is only valid with `method="ucsc_summarize"`. |
    | `zero_inf` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `±inf` values with zero before returning. |
    | `zero_nan` | `bool` | `True` | If `True`, replace `NaN` values with zero before returning. |

    ## Returns

    `np.ndarray` — Aggregated signal values, one per bin.

    ## Raises

    `ValueError` — If `function` is not supported by the chosen
    `method`, or if `method` is not one of `"summarize"`,
    `"ucsc_summarize"`, or `"get_as_array"`.
    """

    if method is None:
        method = 'summarize'

    # We may be dividing by zero in some cases, which raises a warning in
    # NumPy based on the IEEE 754 standard (see
    # http://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/
    #       numpy.seterr.html)
    #
    # That's OK -- we're expecting that to happen sometimes. So temporarily
    # disable this error reporting for the duration of this method.
    orig = np.geterr()['invalid']
    np.seterr(invalid='ignore')

    if (bins is None) or (method == 'get_as_array'):
        bw = self.fileobj
        chrom = interval.chrom
        if isinstance(chrom, str):
            chrom = chrom.encode()
        s = bw.get_as_array(
            chrom,
            interval.start,
            interval.stop,)
        if s is None:
            s = np.zeros((interval.stop - interval.start,))
        else:
            if zero_nan:
                s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
            if zero_inf:
                s[np.isinf(s)] = 0

    elif method == 'ucsc_summarize':
        if function in ['mean', 'min', 'max', 'std', 'coverage']:
            return self.ucsc_summarize(interval, bins, function=function)
        else:
            raise ValueError('function "%s" not supported by UCSC\'s'
                             'bigWigSummary')

    elif method == 'summarize':
        bw = self.fileobj
        s = bw.summarize(
            interval.chrom,
            interval.start,
            interval.stop, bins)

        if s is None:
            s = np.zeros((bins,))
        else:
            if function == 'sum':
                s = s.sum_data
            elif function == 'mean':
                s = s.sum_data / s.valid_count
                if zero_nan:
                    s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
            elif function == 'min':
                s = s.min_val
                if zero_inf:
                    s[np.isinf(s)] = 0
            elif function == 'max':
                s = s.max_val
                if zero_inf:
                    s[np.isinf(s)] = 0
            elif function == 'std':
                s = (s.sum_squares / s.valid_count)
                if zero_nan:
                    s[np.isnan(s)] = 0
            else:
                raise ValueError(
                        'function "%s" not supported by bx-python'
                        % function
                )

    else:
        raise ValueError("method '%s' not in [summarize, ucsc_summarize, get_as_array]" % method)

    # Reset NumPy error reporting
    np.seterr(divide=orig)
    return s

def ucsc_summarize(self, interval, bins=None, function='mean'):
    """
    Summarize a bigWig interval by shelling out to UCSC's `bigWigSummary`.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `interval` | `object` | — | Object with `chrom` (`str`), `start` (`int`), and `stop` (`int`) attributes. |
    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins. If `None`, uses `len(interval)`. |
    | `function` | `str` | `"mean"` | Aggregation type passed to `bigWigSummary -type=`, e.g. `"mean"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"std"`, or `"coverage"`. |

    ## Returns

    `np.ndarray` — Array of shape `(bins,)` with the summarized
    value per bin. Bins with no data from `bigWigSummary` remain `0`.

    ## Raises

    `ValueError` — If the `bigWigSummary` subprocess exits with a
    non-zero, non-`None` return code (other than the "no data" case).
    """
    if bins is None:
        bins = len(interval)
    y = np.zeros(bins)
    cmds = [
        'bigWigSummary',
        self.fn,
        interval.chrom,
        str(interval.start),
        str(interval.stop),
        str(bins),
        '-type=%s' % function]
    p = subprocess.Popen(
        cmds,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
    )

    def gen():
        try:
            for line in p.stdout:
                yield line
        finally:
            if p.poll() is None:
                return
            else:
                p.wait()
                err = p.stderr.read().strip()
                if p.returncode not in (0, None):
                    if err.startswith('no data'):
                        return
                    raise ValueError(
                        "cmds: %s: %s" %
                        (' '.join(cmds), p.stderr.read()))
                if len(err) != 0:
                    sys.stderr.write(err)

    for line in gen():
        for i, x in enumerate(line.split('\t')):
            try:
                y[i] = float(x)
            except ValueError:
                pass
    return np.array(y)

def local_coverage(self, features, *args, **kwargs):
    """
    Compute a binned coverage profile for one or more genomic features.

    Thin wrapper around
    [`_local_coverage`][Pyntegrate.array_helpers._local_coverage]
    using `self.adapter`. When `processes` is set to a positive
    value, a single feature is split into that many chunks, each
    chunk's signal is computed in parallel via `self.array`, and the
    pieces are concatenated back together (optionally rebinned).

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `features` | `interval-like \| str \| list` | — | Feature(s) to compute coverage over. A single feature is required when `processes` is set. |
    | `*args` | — | — | Forwarded to `_local_coverage` (or to `self.array` when `processes` is set). |
    | `processes` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of parallel worker processes for a single large feature. `None`/`0` runs sequentially through `_local_coverage`. |
    | `bins` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of bins to rebin the parallel result into. Only used when `processes` is set. |
    | `**kwargs` | — | — | Forwarded to `_local_coverage` (or to `self.array` when `processes` is set). |

    ## Returns

    `tuple` — `(x, profile)` as returned by `_local_coverage` when
    `processes` is not set; `(x, y)` NumPy coordinate/value arrays
    assembled from parallel chunks (rebinned via `rebin` if `bins`
    is given) when `processes` is set.

    ## Raises

    `ValueError` — If `processes` is set and `features` is a list
    or tuple (parallel mode only supports a single feature).
    """
    processes = kwargs.pop('processes', None)
    if not processes:
        return _local_coverage(self.adapter, features, *args, **kwargs)

    if isinstance(features, (list, tuple)):
        raise ValueError(
            "only single features are supported for parallel "
            "local_coverage")

    bins = kwargs.pop('bins', None)

    features = tointerval(features)
    x = np.arange(features.start, features.stop)
    features = list(split_feature(features, processes))
    ys = self.array(
        features, *args, bins=None, processes=processes, ragged=True,
        **kwargs)
    y = np.column_stack(ys).ravel()
    if bins:
        xi, yi = rebin(x, y, bins)
        return xi, yi
    return x, y

docs.title: mapped_read_count(force=False)
docs.text:
Count the total number of bases covered by the BigWig file.

Uses pyBigWig's header()['nBasesCovered'] — the number of bases that have any interval defined in the file, regardless of that interval's value. This is not the same as the number of bases with non-zero signal: a BigWig that stores explicit zero-value intervals (e.g. produced by bamCoverage without skipping no-coverage regions) counts those bases too, which can inflate the result up to the size of the whole genome.

This value is used as the denominator for CPM normalization throughout pipelines.py (value / (mapped_read_count() / 1e6)) — an inflated count here directly shrinks the normalized signal the pipelines plot.

The result is cached in self._readcount after the first call. If a <file>.mmr sidecar file exists, the count is read from it directly; otherwise the BigWig is scanned and the result is written to <file>.mmr for future use.

def mapped_read_count(self, force=False):
    """
    Count the total number of bases covered by the BigWig file.

    Uses pyBigWig's `header()['nBasesCovered']` — the number of
    bases that have *any* interval defined in the file, regardless
    of that interval's value. **This is not the same as the number
    of bases with non-zero signal**: a BigWig that stores explicit
    zero-value intervals (e.g. produced by `bamCoverage` without
    skipping no-coverage regions) counts those bases too, which can
    inflate the result up to the size of the whole genome.

    This value is used as the denominator for CPM normalization
    throughout `pipelines.py` (`value / (mapped_read_count() / 1e6)`)
    — an inflated count here directly shrinks the normalized signal
    the pipelines plot.

    The result is cached in `self._readcount` after the first call.
    If a `<file>.mmr` sidecar file exists, the count is read from
    it directly; otherwise the BigWig is scanned and the result is
    written to `<file>.mmr` for future use.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `force` | `bool` | `False` | If `True`, ignore the cache and re-count from the file. |

    ## Returns

    `int | None` — Total bases covered (`nBasesCovered`), or `None`
    if the file cannot be opened.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate import genomic_signal

    sig = genomic_signal("chip.bw", "bigwig")
    n = sig.mapped_read_count()
    print(f"Bases covered: {n:,}")
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    Bases covered: 15,243,600
    ```
    """
    if self._readcount and not force:
        return self._readcount

    if os.path.exists(self.fn + '.mmr') and not force:
        for line in open(self.fn + '.mmr'):
            if line.startswith('#'):
                continue
            self._readcount = float(line.strip())
            return self._readcount

    try:
        bwFile = pyBigWig.open(self.fn)
    except RuntimeError:
        return self._readcount
    mapped_reads = bwFile.header()['nBasesCovered']
    if not os.path.exists(self.fn + '.mmr'):
        fout = open(self.fn + '.mmr', 'w')
        fout.write(str(mapped_reads) + '\n')
        fout.close()

    self._readcount = mapped_reads
    return self._readcount

    optionally parallelising the computation. The result is a flat

    | `processes` | `int \| None` | `None` | Number of parallel worker processes. `None` runs sequentially. |

def genome(self):
    """
    Build a genome-size dictionary from the BAM file header.

    Returns a `{chrom: (0, length)}` dictionary compatible with
    `pybedtools` genome operations.

    ## Returns

    `dict[str, tuple[int, int]]` — Mapping of chromosome name to
    `(0, length)` tuples, derived from the BAM `@SQ` header lines.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate import genomic_signal

    bam = genomic_signal("aligned.bam", "bam")
    genome = bam.genome()
    print(genome["chr1"])
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    (0, 248956422)
    ```
    """
    f = self.adapter.fileobj
    d = {}
    for ref, length in zip(f.references, f.lengths):
        d[ref] = (0, length)
    return d

def mapped_read_count(self, force=False):
    """
    Count the total number of mapped reads in the BAM file.

    Uses `samtools view -c -F 0x4` to count only mapped reads.
    The result is cached in `self._readcount` after the first call.
    If a `<file>.mmr` sidecar file exists the count is read from it
    directly; otherwise samtools is run and the result is written to
    `<file>.mmr` for future use.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `force` | `bool` | `False` | If `True`, ignore the cache and re-run samtools. |

    ## Returns

    `int | None` — Total mapped read count, or `None` if samtools
    returns an error.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate import genomic_signal

    bam = genomic_signal("aligned.bam", "bam")
    n = bam.mapped_read_count()
    print(f"Mapped reads: {n:,}")
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    Mapped reads: 42,385,761
    ```
    """
    if self._readcount and not force:
        return self._readcount

    if os.path.exists(self.fn + '.mmr') and not force:
        for line in open(self.fn + '.mmr'):
            if line.startswith('#'):
                continue
            self._readcount = float(line.strip())
            return self._readcount

    cmds = ['samtools', 'view', '-c', '-F', '0x4', self.fn]
    p = subprocess.Popen(
        cmds, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    stdout, stderr = p.communicate()
    if p.returncode != 0:
        sys.stderr.write('samtools says: %s' % stderr.decode(errors='replace'))
        return None
    mapped_reads = int(stdout)

    if not os.path.exists(self.fn + '.mmr'):
        fout = open(self.fn + '.mmr', 'w')
        fout.write(str(mapped_reads) + '\n')
        fout.close()

    self._readcount = mapped_reads
    return self._readcount

def mapped_read_count(self, force=False):
    """
    Count the total number of non-zero intervals in the BigBed file.

    Analogous to `BigWigSignal.mapped_read_count`. The result is
    cached and persisted to a `<file>.mmr` sidecar file.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `force` | `bool` | `False` | If `True`, ignore the cache and re-count from the file. |

    ## Returns

    `int | None` — Total non-zero interval count, or `None` if the
    file cannot be opened.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    from Pyntegrate import genomic_signal

    bb = genomic_signal("peaks.bb", "bigbed")
    print(bb.mapped_read_count())
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    87432
    ```
    """
    if self._readcount and not force:
        return self._readcount

    if os.path.exists(self.fn + '.mmr') and not force:
        for line in open(self.fn + '.mmr'):
            if line.startswith('#'):
                continue
            self._readcount = float(line.strip())
            return self._readcount

    mapped_reads = 0
    try:
        bbFile = pyBigWig.open(self.fn)
        bbFile.header()
    except RuntimeError:
        return self._readcount
    for chrom in bbFile.chroms():
        entries = bbFile.entries(chrom, 0, bbFile.chroms(chrom))
        if entries:
            mapped_reads += len(entries)
    if not os.path.exists(self.fn + '.mmr'):
        fout = open(self.fn + '.mmr', 'w')
        fout.write(str(mapped_reads) + '\n')
        fout.close()

    self._readcount = mapped_reads
    return self._readcount

docs.title: rebin(x, y, nbin)
docs.text:
Linearly interpolate y onto a new uniform grid of nbin points.

Constructs a new x-axis of nbin evenly-spaced points spanning [x.min(), x.max()], then uses linear interpolation to evaluate y at each new point. Useful for normalising genomic signal profiles so that regions of different lengths can be compared or averaged.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description x np.ndarray — Original x-axis coordinates, shape (N,). y np.ndarray — Original y-axis values, shape (N,). nbin int — Number of evenly-spaced points in the output grid.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] — (xi, yi) where xi is the new x-axis of shape (nbin,) and yi contains the interpolated y values at each point of xi, also shape (nbin,).

from Pyntegrate.helpers import rebin

x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.5])
xi, yi = rebin(x, y, nbin=3)
print(xi)
print(np.round(yi, 4))

def rebin(x, y, nbin):
    """
    Linearly interpolate `y` onto a new uniform grid of `nbin` points.

    Constructs a new x-axis of `nbin` evenly-spaced points spanning
    `[x.min(), x.max()]`, then uses linear interpolation to evaluate
    `y` at each new point. Useful for normalising genomic signal
    profiles so that regions of different lengths can be compared or
    averaged.

    ## Parameters

    | Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
    |-----------|------|---------|-------------|
    | `x` | `np.ndarray` | — | Original x-axis coordinates, shape `(N,)`. |
    | `y` | `np.ndarray` | — | Original y-axis values, shape `(N,)`. |
    | `nbin` | `int` | — | Number of evenly-spaced points in the output grid. |

    ## Returns

    `tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]` — `(xi, yi)` where `xi` is the new
    x-axis of shape `(nbin,)` and `yi` contains the interpolated y
    values at each point of `xi`, also shape `(nbin,)`.

    ## Examples

    ```python
    import numpy as np
    from Pyntegrate.helpers import rebin

    x = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
    y = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.5])
    xi, yi = rebin(x, y, nbin=3)
    print(xi)
    print(np.round(yi, 4))
    ```

    **Output:**
    ```
    [0. 2. 4.]
    [0.   0.5  1.5]
    ```
    """
    xi = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), nbin)
    return xi, np.interp(xi, x, y)

The last chunk may contain fewer than n elements if the total length of f is not a multiple of n. This is used internally to distribute genomic features across parallel worker processes.
